title: Who Gave You This Key?
summary: OAuth as the only topic, slowed down: the valet key that lets an app act for you inside another app without your password. Walked through an Add to Slack install step by step, the Slack developer pages where you register an app (client ID, client secret, redirect URL, scopes), the Microsoft sign-in behind every Power Automate connection, and a customer call where an integration died because the person who connected it left. With an API key callback and Zendesk retiring API tokens in favor of OAuth.

topics.name: OAuth
topics.blurb: The valet key: an app gets a limited, short-lived, revocable token to act for you inside another app, approved on the real provider's consent screen, without ever seeing your password

topics.name: API keys (callback)
topics.blurb: An API key identifies an app acting as itself; OAuth adds which person approved it and exactly what it may do. Client secrets are guarded like API keys

sources.title: Slack Developer Docs: Installing with OAuth (authorize URL, 10-minute code, oauth.v2.access, xoxb bot token)
Zendesk: Announcing the removal of API tokens as an authentication method for API requests

glossary.definition: The public name tag an app gets when you register it with an OAuth provider like Slack or Google. Safe to show; it says which app is asking, while the client secret proves it.

The exact address on an app's site where the provider sends the user back after they approve access, carrying the one-time code. Must be registered ahead of time so codes can't be sent to an attacker's site.

The saved sign-in a Power Automate connector uses to act as you in a service like Outlook or SharePoint. It is your OAuth key with your name on it; 'fix connection' means signing in again to get a fresh one.
A user account created just to own an integration's connection, not tied to any one employee, so the integration keeps working when people leave or change roles.
A way of using OAuth where an app gets a token for itself using its client ID and secret, with no person signing in or approving. Used for behind-the-scenes, server-to-server integrations.

sections.heading: Two keys you already carry
sections.body:
Morning, and welcome to Mind the Gap. This is episode ten, and it's Thursday.

One topic today, the one I promised yesterday: OAuth. It got squeezed into episode three alongside webhooks and some news, which was too much for one drive. So today it gets the whole commute, and it's built almost entirely out of real examples.

Quick callback first, because OAuth makes the most sense sitting right next to something you already know: the A-P-I key from episode five. Remember the fuel card picture. An A-P-I key is a company fuel card for a program. It says which app is calling, so the service can let it in, count its calls, and bill the right account. It identifies a program, not a person, and you guard it like a password.

That works great when a program is acting as itself. This podcast's script calling a text-to-speech service is a program doing its own job. But a huge amount of software does something different. It acts on behalf of a person, inside somebody else's product. A notes app that posts into your Slack. A scheduling tool that reads your calendar. A Power Automate flow that sends email from your Outlook. In every one of those, the question isn't just which app is this. It's which app is this, which person said it was okay, and what exactly did they say it could do. An A-P-I key can't answer that. OAuth can.

sections.heading: The valet key, slowed down
sections.body:
Here's the picture, and we'll go slower than last time.

You pull up to a restaurant with valet parking. You need a stranger to do one job with your car: park it. You don't hand over your house keys, your garage opener and your full car key. You hand over the valet key. It starts the car and opens the driver's door. It doesn't open the trunk or the glove box. And when you leave, you take it back.

OAuth, spelled O-A-U-T-H and said oh-auth, is the valet key system for software. In plain English: it lets you give one app limited access to your stuff inside another app, without ever giving it your password, and you can take that access back whenever you want.

There are always four players, so let's name them once, using the restaurant.

You are the car owner. You own the stuff.

The app that wants access is the valet. In OAuth language that's the client.

The place where your stuff lives, like Slack or Google or Microsoft, is the car. And that same company runs the valet stand, the desk that checks who you are and hands out keys.

The key itself is called an access token. It's a long string of characters, a lot like an A-P-I key, but with three differences that matter. It's tied to a person, not just an app. It only opens certain doors, and each door is called a scope, like read your calendar or post messages. And it's short-lived and revocable, which just means it expires on its own and you can cancel it early.

Now, how the valet gets the key, which people call the OAuth dance. Four steps, and you've done the visible half of this a hundred times without noticing.

Step one. You click a button in the app, something like Connect your calendar. The app sends your browser to the real provider, Google or Slack or Microsoft. You type your password there, on their real website, and nowhere else.

Step two. The provider shows a consent screen: this app wants to do these specific things. That list is the scopes. You click allow.

Step three. The provider sends your browser back to the app, carrying a one-time claim ticket called an authorization code. It's not the key. It's a coat check stub, and it expires within minutes.

Step four happens out of sight, server to server. The app's server takes that claim ticket, adds its own secret, called the client secret, and trades both for the real access token. Needing both is the safety trick. Someone who steals the claim ticket from the browser can't use it without the app's secret, and the secret never touches the browser.

From then on, every time the app calls the provider's A-P-I, it puts that access token in the request header, the same slot where an A-P-I key goes. The provider sees the token and knows: this app, for this person, allowed to do these things.

That's the idea. Now let's watch it happen in places you'll recognize.

sections.heading: Add to Slack
sections.body:
First example: the Add to Slack button.

Say your team signs up for a meeting notes tool, an app that listens to your calls and posts a summary into a Slack channel afterward. On the tool's settings page there's a button that says Add to Slack. Here's everything that happens when your manager clicks it.

Click one sends your manager's browser to a page on Slack's own website. That address carries a few things the notes app tucked in: its client I-D, which is just the app's public name tag, the list of scopes it wants, and a redirect U-R-L, which is the address on the notes app's site where Slack should send the browser back afterward.

Slack checks that your manager is signed in, then shows the approval screen. It names the workspace and lists what the app is asking for in plain words. Something like: send messages as the app, and view basic information about public channels. Your manager reads it and clicks Allow.

Slack sends the browser back to that redirect U-R-L with a temporary code attached. Slack's docs say that code expires after ten minutes. Your manager sees a page that says connected, and as far as they're concerned, they're done.

But behind the scenes, the notes app's server takes that code and calls Slack directly, sending the code plus its client I-D and client secret. Slack checks all three match and hands back a token. For an app like this, it's a bot token, which starts with the letters x-o-x-b. That's the same kind of bot token from the Slack example in episode six, and now you know where it actually comes from. The notes app stores it on its server, guarded like an A-P-I key.

After the next meeting, the notes app calls Slack's A-P-I to post a message, with that bot token in the header. Slack sees the token, checks the scopes, sees that posting messages is allowed, and the summary shows up in the channel.

Notice what never happened. Your manager never typed a Slack password into the notes app. The notes app can post messages, but it never got a scope to read everyone's direct messages, so it can't. And if your team stops using the tool, an admin removes the app in Slack and the token stops working, with no password changes for anybody.

sections.heading: Building the other side
sections.body:
Second example flips your seat. Now you're the one building the app that wants in. This is the practical how-it's-done part, and Slack is a clean place to see it.

You go to Slack's developer site and create a new app. On the app's Basic Information page, Slack shows you two values you'll use constantly. The client I-D, which is public and fine to show, because it's just the name tag. And the client secret, which Slack hides behind a show button, because it's exactly like an A-P-I key: it proves the request is really coming from your app's server. It goes in your server's settings, or a secrets vault, never into your code, and never into a web page.

Then you open a page called OAuth and Permissions. Two things go there. First, your redirect U-R-L, the exact address where Slack is allowed to send people back. Slack only sends people back to addresses you listed here, and it requires a secure H-T-T-P-S address. That's a safety rule: if an attacker tricked Slack into sending the claim ticket to their own site, they'd be one step closer to a token. Locking down the return address stops that. Second, the scopes your app needs. You pick them from a list, and the advice from episode three still holds: ask for the fewest you can. Every extra scope is one more line on the consent screen, and one more thing a customer's security team will question.

Now put it together. Your Add to Slack button points at Slack's authorize page with your client I-D, your scopes and your redirect U-R-L. A user clicks it, approves, and lands back on your redirect U-R-L with a code. Your server swaps the code plus your client secret for a token, saves it, and from then on calls Slack's A-P-I with it.

Google, Microsoft, Salesforce, Zoom, they all follow this same shape. The page names change, but you'll always register an app, get a client I-D and client secret, list your redirect U-R-Ls, and choose scopes. Learn it once in Slack and you'll recognize it everywhere.

sections.heading: The sign-in box inside Power Automate
sections.body:
Third example, from your internship.

When you build a Power Automate flow and add your first Outlook action, like send an email, Power Automate doesn't ask you to type your password into a box inside the flow. Instead it says you need to sign in to create a connection. You click sign in, a Microsoft sign-in window pops up, you sign in there, and if your company requires it, you approve on your phone. Sometimes you'll see a permissions screen listing what's being requested. Then the window closes and the action turns ready.

That pop-up is the OAuth dance. The connector is the client. Microsoft's sign-in service is the valet stand. And the thing Power Automate saved, which it calls a connection, is basically your valet key with your name on it, stored so your flow can keep using it later at three in the morning when you're asleep.

That last part explains something that confuses a lot of people. The connection belongs to the person who signed in. When your flow sends an email, it sends as you, because it's using your key. If you later change your password, or your account gets turned off, that connection can stop working, and the flow starts failing even though nobody touched the flow itself. In Power Automate you'll see the connection marked as needing attention, with an option to fix it, which really just means do the dance again and get a fresh key.

The other piece you'll bump into is refresh tokens. Access tokens are deliberately short-lived, often around an hour. So how does a flow keep working for months? Along with the access token, the provider usually hands out a refresh token, a longer-lived key whose only job is to quietly get new access tokens without bugging you. Power Automate does that refreshing behind the scenes. You only notice when the refresh token itself gets cancelled, and then you're back to clicking fix connection.

sections.heading: The integration that died when Dana left
sections.body:
Fourth example, and this one is pure Solutions Engineer.

You're on a call with a customer. Their sales team's call recordings used to flow automatically from your product into their Salesforce. On Monday, it stopped. Nothing changed, they say.

You ask the question that OAuth teaches you to ask: who connected it? There's a pause. Then: Dana did. Dana was the sales ops manager. Dana left the company last Friday.

That's your answer. When the integration was set up, Dana clicked connect, signed in, and approved the scopes. The token your product holds was Dana's valet key. When IT turned off Dana's account on Friday, the provider stopped honoring the keys issued for that person. Now every call your product makes comes back with a four-oh-one, unauthorized: I don't know who you are anymore. Callback to episode six: a four-oh-one means the credential is missing, wrong, expired or cancelled.

Here's how you walk it with the customer.

Step one, confirm it. Look at your product's error log or integration status page for four-oh-ones starting right around when Dana's account was disabled.

Step two, reconnect. Someone with the right access does the dance again. Then whatever didn't sync since Friday needs to be caught up, either by a resync button or by pulling it through the A-P-I.

Step three, prevent it. Recommend they connect with a dedicated integration account, a user created just for this connection that doesn't belong to any one employee, or use an app-level setup if the provider offers one. Then people can come and go without breaking anything.

And here's a cousin of this problem you'll also see. Your product ships a new feature that needs one more scope, say, permission to write notes back, not just read. The old token doesn't have it. So that new call comes back four-oh-three, forbidden: I know who you are, but you're not allowed to do this. The fix isn't a new password. Someone has to approve the app again so the new scope gets added to the key.

Four-oh-one, the key is dead. Four-oh-three, the key works but doesn't open that door. If you can say that calmly on a call, you'll resolve these in minutes.

sections.heading: Where this lands on your desk
sections.body:
So where does OAuth actually show up for you?

On sales and security reviews, the customer's security team will ask: what scopes does your app request, and why? They'll read the consent screen line by line. If your product asks to read all mail when it only needs calendar events, that can stall a deal. Knowing your product's scope list, and having a one-sentence reason for each scope, is real leverage.

In demos, the Connect button is often the first thing you click. When the consent screen pops up, that's a great moment to say: notice you're signing in on Microsoft's page, not ours. We never see your password, you can see exactly what we can touch, and your admin can cut us off anytime. Non-technical buyers hear that as safe and in control.

In troubleshooting, most broken-integration calls come down to a handful of OAuth stories: the person who connected it left, someone revoked the app, a password or security policy changed, or a new feature needs a scope the old key doesn't have. The status codes tell you which.

In interviews, the classic question is: what's the difference between an A-P-I key and OAuth? The strong answer: an A-P-I key identifies an app acting as itself. OAuth lets an app act for a specific person, with limited permissions the person approved, through short-lived tokens that can be revoked, without the app ever seeing the password.

And if you end up in data or cloud work, almost every connector you set up, pulling from Salesforce, Google Analytics, or HubSpot into a warehouse, starts with this same sign-in and approve step.

sections.heading: Zendesk retires its API tokens
sections.body:
One news item, because it's a near-perfect example of today's topic.

Zendesk, the customer support software a lot of companies run their help desks on, is retiring A-P-I tokens for its main support A-P-Is and moving everyone to OAuth. A-P-I tokens there work like the A-P-I keys from episode five: a long-lived secret an admin creates in a settings page and pastes into an integration.

According to Zendesk's announcement, it's happening in phases. Starting this past July, tokens that went unused for thirty days began switching off. Then, on October twenty-seventh, less than three weeks from now, nobody can create new A-P-I tokens at all. Existing ones keep working until April thirtieth, twenty twenty-seven, when they're all shut off for good, and Zendesk says there's no extension.

What Zendesk tells customers to do is exactly today's setup: create an OAuth client in their admin settings, get access tokens instead, and update the integration to use them. They mention two ways to get tokens. One is the authorization code flow you heard all morning, with a person approving. The other, called client credentials, is a version where an app gets a token for itself with no person in the loop, for behind-the-scenes integrations.

Why this matters to you: picture being a Solutions Engineer at any company that integrates with Zendesk right now. Your customers will be calling to ask whether your integration is going to break next spring, and the right answer involves every word from today: client, scopes, tokens, and who approves.

sections.heading: Pocket version
sections.body:
Here's the pocket version.

OAuth is the valet key system for software. It lets one app do limited things in another app on your behalf, without ever seeing your password, and you can take that access back anytime.

The app sends you to the real provider, you sign in there, you approve a list of scopes on the consent screen, the app gets a short-lived claim ticket, and its server trades that ticket plus its client secret for an access token. The token goes in the header of every A-P-I call. A refresh token quietly gets new ones.

You saw it today in an Add to Slack button, in the Slack developer pages where you'd build one yourself, in the sign-in window behind every Power Automate connection, and in a customer call where an integration died because the person who connected it left. Four-oh-one, the key is dead. Four-oh-three, the key doesn't open that door.

When you're parked, open the text version and mark how this one landed, and leave a note if anything's still fuzzy.

Saturday's recap will come back to this week's topics with fresh examples. Tomorrow, a step out of the web and into the cloud: infrastructure, platform and software as a service, three ways of renting someone else's computers. Drive safe.
